Gold can, of course, enter into various chemical compounds in which these qualities seem at first to disappear. What, after all, does a bar of pure gold appear to have in common with some white powder? But the chemist knows that the essential qualities remain unchanged. He looks for them and finds them where an ordinary person cannot see them.
Chemistry can therefore exist as a science only because such “identical” chemical qualities exist—that is, because there is non-dialectical existence, at least in its chemical aspect.
In this sense, the biologist is no different from the chemist or physicist.

Aristotle, for example, believed that the “types” of animals and plants remained eternally the same, just like the physicist’s “atoms” or “electrons.” With Lamarck and Darwin, biology came to regard these “types” as changing and “transforming” into one another, either gradually or by leaps. But this changes nothing essential.

When a modern zoologist describes, say, a cat, he is still looking for its “unchanging” characteristics: the qualities that always belong to it equally insofar as it is a cat. Those are the only qualities he seeks.

He may find it difficult to say exactly when the “pre-cat” became a “true cat.” But a chemist faces the same kind of difficulty when asked to say exactly when a burning tree stops being a tree and becomes charcoal.

Charcoal nevertheless has, for the chemist, “unchanging” qualities—qualities “identical” with themselves—even though contemporary physics has shown that the chemical “elements” can transform into one another.

And what applies to the existence of these “identical” qualities also applies to the transformation of species in Lamarck, Darwin, or De Vries: what changes is the classification of the “identical” biological qualities of living things.

Whatever natural “thing” we examine, then, we will always find in it a firm backbone made up of its “essential” qualities, which remain “eternally unchanged.” The presence of these qualities allows us to say that the existence of the thing is governed by the characteristic—or, in philosophical language, the category—of identity, because the thing always remains what it is.

Philosophers have used many different words for this “identical” backbone. It has been called the “idea” or eidos, the “reflection” or “image” of the thing in Plato, the entelechy or “actuality” of the thing in Aristotle, its “nature,” its “substantial form,” its “essence” in Scholasticism, and so on. The “thing” itself, insofar as it is identical, has also been called a “substance” or given some other name.
The words are obviously not what matters.
What matters is that the “nature” or, say, the “essence” of a thing is nothing more than the complete set of its “essential” qualities or characteristics, in the strict sense of the term.

The “thing” as a whole may change. It may even come into existence and disappear. But its “nature” or “essence” remains eternally unchanged. That is why the thing itself always remains “what it is”: always identical with itself.

Its “essence” is like the axis of a spinning top. The axis not only remains “unchanged”; it also stabilizes the top itself, forcing it to repeat “eternally” the same rotational movement—the movement that defines it as a spinning top, regardless of its shape, color, material, and so on.
It is also important that when we speak about a natural thing, or “designate” it, what we have in mind is precisely its essence.
The same “essence” is both the “nature” of the thing itself and the meaning of the word that designates it—and thereby “reveals” it to consciousness, thought, and knowledge.
It makes no difference whether we want to “define” the meaning of a word or the thing itself. In either case we must list its “essential” qualities.

Our words—with the exception of “proper names,” which are not really “words” at all but linguistic “gestures,” pointing to one particular thing in the same way as an extended finger or a nod—do not refer to the “concrete” or “real” thing as it actually exists here and now. They refer to the “abstract” essence of things: to the set of their “essential” characteristics.
The word “cat,” for example, refers both to this cat running across the street at this moment and to the “cat in general” studied by zoology.

More generally, scientific words and scientific discourse—that is, natural science itself—differ from ordinary words and the speech of non-specialists about nature only in this respect: science consciously tries to separate the essential qualities from the inessential ones. It ignores the inessential qualities and tries, as far as possible, to give a complete account of the essential ones.

Of course, when a scientist—or for that matter an ordinary person—speaks about a “thing,” he does not merely separate it from everything else. He also studies its connections: the reciprocal relations or interactions between the isolated thing and other equally isolated things.
Ultimately, he tries to determine the “place”—the topos, as Aristotle would say—of each thing within the totality of things, within the natural world, within the Greek cosmos.
But what he studies is not the interaction of the concrete things themselves. He studies the interaction of their essences.

And it is only because these essences are identical—that is, eternally unchanging—that the scientist can discover “scientific” laws: unchanging laws governing their interactions. Since the interaction of things constitutes the “world,” he thereby discovers the “laws” governing the world itself.

Conversely, if one begins one’s reasoning from the world as a whole, from the cosmos—as the Greeks and Scholastics did, and as some contemporary biologists and physicists influenced by “relativity” partly do—then the scientist will try to define things and their interactions by determining the eternal or “identical” place each thing occupies within an eternally unchanging world.

But in that case, too, what he discovers is not the “thing itself” but only its identical “nature” or “essence.” And what he discovers in their relations is not the relations themselves but only the eternally unchanging “laws” that govern them.
Seen from this point of view, we can say that natural things have an “identical” essence precisely because they occupy, so to speak, a “permanent” place in an unchanging cosmos.
We might say, for example, that “fish in general” have a fish-like form because they always live in water, while “birds” have their characteristic form because they fly through the air, and so on.

To sum up: let us call anything that exists non-dialectically a “thing” or “substance”—both the natural world as a whole, the “cosmos,” and each individual thing within it. We can then say that every thing has an eternally unchanging or identical nature or essence, definable as the complete set of its “essential” qualities or characteristics.
We can also say, if we like, that this essence is conditioned by the “place” the thing occupies among all the other things in the natural cosmos.
Or, more briefly: the existence of all things taken together, and of each individual thing taken separately, is ultimately governed by the fundamental category of identity.

There can be no doubt that the category of identity is present in everything that exists. If everything changed completely and continuously, never remaining in place and never being “identical” in any respect, we could never speak about anything at all. We would literally have nothing to say, since one can obviously speak only about something that “exists” in some way.
The only question is whether some other fundamental category is also present in what exists.

Hegel discovered precisely such a second fundamental category and called it negativity. He calls any existence in which this second category is present “dialectical,” or simply calls it “the dialectic.”
Dialectic therefore necessarily contains at least two categories: identity and negativity. And the second does not merely exist alongside the first. It dominates it.
It is precisely this dominance of negativity that makes an existence dialectical. This is why negativity can be called the root or driving force of dialectic.
Now that we know what “identity” is, we can ask what “negativity” consists in.

As the word itself suggests, negativity is the direct opposite of identity. Identity preserves the identity of a thing—its equality with itself, its eternal immutability. Negativity, by contrast, negates all of this.
But every negation necessarily presupposes what it negates.

To negate, there must always be “something” to negate, and this positive something must exist independently of the negation and before it. Negativity therefore presupposes identity, along with the identical—that is, non-dialectical—existence governed by identity.
Taken entirely by itself, outside identical existence, “negativity” does not exist at all. It is the “non-being” or “nothingness” about which there is simply nothing to say, because it is not.

Yet for some reason that admits of no further explanation, and at this point blocks any deeper analysis, this nothingness enters positive, identical existence and penetrates it, so to speak, from within. There it becomes effective or “active.”
And what is active is, by that very fact, effective or actual.
By entering the non-dialectical existence governed by identity, and by acting within it and upon it, negative or negating nothingness thereby becomes an “active” or “effective nothingness.”
This “active” or “effective” nothingness—something that is therefore in a certain sense “real,” while still being negative or negating—is precisely what we call negativity.
As I have already said, negativity is not merely present and active within dialectic. It also dominates identity there.
And although it is only this dominance of negativity that transforms identical existence into dialectical existence, negativity itself is negativity only because it dominates identity.
In general, the negation of “identity” is otherness. To deny that a thing is identical with itself is simply to say that it changes.

But as we have seen, the fact that natural things change is perfectly compatible with their identity. In such cases we can say that the category of “otherness” remains subordinate to the category of identity. It is therefore an entirely non-dialectical category, one that governs the “inessential” qualities of non-dialectical things.
Negativity, by contrast, is not subordinate to identity. It dominates it.
That means it produces changes in the very “nature” or identical “essence” of a thing—in the complete set of its essential qualities.

But since “nature” or “essence” is, by definition, eternally unchanging, we have to say that a dialectical being has no “nature” or “essence” at all. And that is why we do not call such a being a “thing.”
The human being is this dialectical being.

We can therefore say that a human being is nothing other than negativity existing within the natural world and acting within it. Negativity, in turn, is nothing other than the human being—or humanity.
Human beings therefore have no eternally unchanging essence. They can change even in their essential qualities.
We will see in the Phenomenology how negativity operates. For now, I will give only two examples.

From the beginning of its historical existence, humanity has been divided into two “classes”: slaves and masters. An individual had necessarily to be either master or slave, insofar as we consider him as a historical human being, just as he had necessarily to be either female or male insofar as we consider his animal reality.

In one form or another, this division into classes persisted throughout the centuries of human history. We can therefore say without exaggeration that “mastery” and “slavery” became essential qualities of human existence.
And yet there now exists in the USSR a socialist society that had never existed before, a society containing neither masters nor slaves but free and equal citizens.

This therefore provides factual proof—against bourgeois thinkers who denied the dialectical character of human beings—that the supposedly “eternally unchanging” human “nature” or “essence” can itself change without human beings ceasing to be human.
It changed under the influence of revolutionary struggle, which, as we will see, is the first and primary manifestation of negativity.

We saw that the nature or “essence” of a non-dialectical thing is determined by its “place” in the cosmos. Human beings, as animals, also possess such a nature. The human being is a “land-dwelling animal.” The human body is shaped by this fact and, like the body of every land animal, is poorly adapted to living underwater or in the air.
That is how the human body was, is, and will remain.

And yet, insofar as human beings inhabit a technical world—that is, insofar as they are human beings in the proper sense—they occupy the air, notably by means of airplanes, and live underwater, for example in submarines.
They achieve this through technical work, which, as we will see, is a fundamental but secondary manifestation of negativity.
Human beings do not grow wings or fins. Their bodies remain what they are. And yet human beings cease to be merely “land animals” and become, in addition, animals of “water” and “air.”

The existence of a dialectical being is therefore not finally and irrevocably determined by the “natural” or “essential” place it occupies in the world. It can change the human “nature” determined by that place and, so to speak, cross the boundaries prescribed for it by the world.

This means that a dialectical or “negative” being changes not only in the way a non-dialectical thing changes—that is, as a result of interactions imposed on it from outside, through the effects of all the other things in the cosmos. It also changes from within itself, without any external necessity, or, as philosophy puts it, “spontaneously” or “freely.”
We can therefore say that a dialectical being has no “nature” given to it once and for all by who knows whom—God—or by who knows what—the “cosmos,” “nature,” and so on.
Instead, we must say that it creates or produces itself, along with its own “essential” qualities, and that it changes itself in an essential way.
This self-creation and this creative—that is, essential—self-transformation are themselves manifestations or acts of negativity.
More precisely, insofar as negativity is not nothing but something, it is nothing other than this essential self-creation, this transformation of dialectical being.
So, to define negativity, we can use Hegel’s somewhat paradoxical formula and say that negativity is the capacity of a dialectical being “not to be what it is and to be what it is not.”
This capacity also distinguishes a dialectical being from a non-dialectical thing, which always remains equal to itself and can therefore be only what it is.
Since, as we will see, negating desire is the first and simplest manifestation of negativity, we can modify Hegel’s definition and remove some of its paradoxical form.
We can say that negativity gives a dialectical being the ability not to want to be what it is, and to want to be what it is not.
And it is easy to see that this desire to negate one’s own “essence” or “nature” is characteristic of human beings, and of human beings alone.
There is an old Jewish joke.
A son is reading a book and asks his father:
“A woodpecker?” the father replies. “Oh, a woodpecker iz a fisch.”
“What are you talking about? It says here that it sits in a tree!”
“Well,” says the father, “es iz a meshugener fisch”—it’s a fish that has lost its mind.

Strictly speaking, if we saw a fish so much as trying—or wanting—to live the life of a bird, we would have to say either that it had lost its mind or that it was really a human being that happened to look like a fish.
But madness is an illness, and nature removes sick individuals from its environment by killing them. So there will be no fish that flies and no bird that lives underwater.
If a human being actually becomes amphibious, then, this means that this animal has “lost its mind” and yet has still managed to survive within the natural world.

The titanic power—work and struggle—that allowed human beings to impose their “madness” on the natural world, and not only to survive in that world despite this madness but to alter the world in accordance with it, is precisely what Hegel calls negativity.
This human negativity is expressed with unusual precision and radical force by one of the characters in Kurt Weill and Bertolt Brecht’s opera Mahagonny.
Someone tries to shake him morally by saying, as people often do, “Be a man!”
“But I don’t want to be a man at all” (Ich will ja gar kein Mensch sein).

And we know that such a radically “negating” desire is not always an unrealizable Nietzschean dream of “superhumanity.” It can also take the form of a kind of negative realization in Kirillov-like suicide: suicide without a cause, in the natural sense of the word.

In any case, dialectic—dialectical existence or dialectical being—is produced by the dominance of negativity over identity. In other words, it depends on a being’s ability to create itself, or to change “spontaneously”—that is, “freely,” independently of “physical” causes—its own essential qualities and characteristics: precisely those features that, in a non-dialectical thing, would be called its “nature” or “essence.”
But I repeat: this dominance of negativity over identity necessarily presupposes that identity itself is also present in dialectic—in dialectical existence and in the dialectical being.
In other words, a dialectical being necessarily contains at least two fundamental categories.
But if both are present, there must also be a third and final fundamental dialectical category: the category that unites them, which Hegel calls totality (Totalität).
Identity forces a thing to remain the same. Negativity allows it to change essentially.
Because a dialectical being contains both identity and negativity, it must therefore remain the same despite its essential changes, and it must change essentially despite remaining the same.

The difference between a Greek slave and a free citizen of the socialist state may be far more “essential” than, say, the difference between a snail and a chimpanzee. Yet the slave and the citizen are both human beings.
